title: Slope fields and equilibria
objectives: Sketch a slope field and classify equilibria as stable or unstable.

screens.title: Follow the slopes
screens.prose: Each short segment shows the slope that $y' = t - y$ demands at that point. The curve from your start follows the segments. Drag the start up and down the left edge.

derive.caption: From $y(0)$ = {{fixed(P.y, 2)}}: at $t = 4$ the path is at {{fixed(values.TEndY, 3)}}

screens.question: What do the paths do as $t$ grows?

options.text: They close in on one straight line

options.why: Level paths need slope 0, but at $y = 0$ the slope is $t$, which grows.
Drag two starts far apart: by $t = 4$ they almost meet.

options.text: They head to the line $y = t$
options.why: On $y = t$ the slope is 0, so a path there would flatten off it.

feedback.correct: Every path is drawn onto the same straight line.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try a start at 2.5 and one at $-1.5$, and compare where they end.

explain.text: Whatever the start, the paths merge onto one line, which rises with slope 1. We find it on the next screen.

screens.title: A straight-line solution
screens.prose: On $y = t - 1$ the slope is 1, and $t - y = 1$ too, so the line is itself a solution. Every solution is $y = t - 1 + Ce^{-t}$: the gap to the line dies away as $e^{-t}$. The drawn path starts at $y(0) = 0$.
screens.question: What is $y(1)$ on that path, to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fit $C$ from $y(0) = -1 + C = 0$.

byKey.line: You read the line, $t - 1 = 0$ at $t = 1$. The path still sits $e^{-1}$ above it.

explain.text: $C = 1$, so $y = t - 1 + e^{-t}$ and $y(1) = e^{-1} = 0.3679$. The gap $e^{-t}$ shrinks, so the path joins the line.

screens.title: Slopes that depend only on height
screens.prose: Now take $y' = (y - 1)(y - 3)$. The right side has no $t$: the equation is **autonomous**. So every column of the field looks the same. Drag the start and look for paths that never move.
screens.question: Select all that apply: at which heights is a path flat for ever?

options.why: At $y = 2$ the slope is $(1)(-1) = -1$: the steepest descent, not flat.
At $y = 0$ the slope is $(-1)(-3) = 3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A flat path needs $(y - 1)(y - 3) = 0$.

explain.text: Where $f(y) = 0$ the slope is 0 in every column, so $y = 1$ and $y = 3$ are constant solutions. Between them the slope is negative; outside, positive.

screens.title: Which way the paths go
screens.prose: Drag the start to just below 3, at $y(0) = 2.9$. Then try a start just above 3. The caption reads where the path is at $t = 5$, when it is still on the chart.
screens.question: From $y(0) = 2.9$, what is $y(5)$, to 3 decimal places?

hints.text: About 1.002: the path falls to the lower equilibrium.

feedback.correct: The path drops from 2.9 and settles just above 1: $y(5) \approx 1.0017$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the start at 2.9 and read the caption.

byKey.three: You expected it to return to 3. Below 3 the slope is negative, so it falls away.
byKey.start: You read the start. The path moves: below 3 the slope is negative.

explain.text: Just below 3 the slope is negative, so the path falls all the way to 1: $y(5) \approx 1.0017$. Just above 3 it runs off the top. Paths leave 3 and arrive at 1.

screens.title: The phase line
screens.prose: Drop the time axis. The column of arrows is the **phase line**: up where $f(y) > 0$, down where $f(y) < 0$. The curve is $f(y)$ drawn sideways, with $f = 0$ dashed. At $y = 1$ it crosses from positive to negative.
screens.question: What is $f'(1)$ for $f(y) = (y - 1)(y - 3)$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Expand $f = y^2 - 4y + 3$ and differentiate.

byKey.zero: That is $f(1)$, the value. The derivative is the slope of $f$.

explain.text: $f'(1) = -2 < 0$: just below 1 the arrows point up, just above they point down, so paths close in on 1. At 3, $f'(3) = 2 > 0$ and the arrows point away.

screens.title: Another phase line
screens.prose: For $y' = 1 - y^2$ the equilibria are $y = -1$ and $y = 1$. Read the arrows on each side of each one, then check with $f'(y) = -2y$.
screens.question: Which equilibrium attracts nearby paths?

options.why: Just below $-1$, $f < 0$, so paths move down and away. $f'(-1) = 2 > 0$.
Check the arrows below $-1$: they point away from it.
Between the two the arrows point up, towards $+1$.

hints.text: Look at the arrows on both sides of $+1$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the arrows just above and just below each point.

explain.text: Arrows point towards $+1$ from both sides and away from $-1$. That matches $f'(1) = -2 < 0$ and $f'(-1) = 2 > 0$.

screens.title: The derivative test
screens.prose:
For an autonomous equation $y' = f(y)$, an equilibrium $y^*$ has $f(y^*) = 0$. Then:

$$f'(y^*) < 0 \Rightarrow \text{stable}, \qquad f'(y^*) > 0 \Rightarrow \text{unstable}.$$

Near $y^*$, $f(y) \approx f'(y^*)(y - y^*)$, so a small gap $u = y - y^*$ nearly obeys lesson 1's $u' = f'(y^*)u$.
screens.question: The logistic has $f(P) = 0.8P(1 - P/10000)$. What is $f'(K)$ at $K = 10{,}000$?

byKey.plus: That is $f'(0)$, at the other equilibrium, which is unstable.
byKey.zero: That is $f(K)$. The test uses the slope $f'$.

explain.text: $f'(K) = -0.8$, so the gap to $K$ shrinks as $e^{-0.8t}$: $K$ is stable. $f'(0) = 0.8 > 0$, so 0 is unstable, as the broker's clients showed.

screens.title: Not the sign, not the bigger one
screens.prose: Take $y' = y^2 - 4$, with equilibria $-2$ and $+2$. A colleague says the positive one must be the stable one. Another checks the sign of $f$ at each point. Read the arrows instead.
screens.question: Tap the stable equilibrium.

hints.text: At an equilibrium $f = 0$, so look at the slope of $f$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at the arrows just above and just below each point.

byKey.p2: You picked the positive one. Above 2 the arrows point up, below it down: paths leave $+2$.

explain.text: $f'(y) = 2y$, so $f'(-2) = -4$ and $f'(2) = 4$. $f$ is 0 at every equilibrium, so its sign decides nothing. Being positive decides nothing either.

screens.title: Equilibria in NumPy
screens.prose: For a polynomial $f$, `np.roots` finds the equilibria; keep the real ones. Then classify each by the sign of $f$ a little either side, which still works when $f'(y^*) = 0$.
screens.question: Complete `equilibrium_type` and `equilibria`.

widget.how: Check runs 9 hidden tests: the type as text, and the roots as a sorted list within 1e-9. The first run loads NumPy, which takes a few seconds.

hints.text: Evaluate $f$ just left and just right of $y^*$.
Up then down is stable; down then up is unstable; anything else is semi-stable.
Keep roots with `abs(r.imag) < 1e-9`, round the real parts and sort.

feedback.correct: Signs either side classify every equilibrium, including the semi-stable ones.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Compare the signs of `f(y_star - h)` and `f(y_star + h)`, and drop complex roots.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace each `...` with code that returns.

explain.text:
Positive on the left and negative on the right means paths close in. Same sign on both sides is semi-stable.

```python
left, right = f(y_star - h), f(y_star + h)
if left > 0 and right < 0:
    return "stable"
```

screens.title: A tipping point
screens.prose: A trading venue's market share $x$ follows $x' = x(1 - x)(x - 0.3)$: liquidity attracts liquidity. The equilibria are 0, 30% and 100%. The chart starts two venues at 25% and 35%.
screens.question: A venue holds 25% today. Where does its share head?

options.why: 30% is an equilibrium, but $f'(0.3) = 0.21 > 0$: it repels.
That is where the 35% venue goes. Below 30% the slope is negative.
25% is not an equilibrium: $f(0.25) < 0$.

hints.text: Negative slope below 30%: the share falls to 0.

feedback.correct: Below the tipping point at 30% the share drains to 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the sign of $x' $ at $x = 0.25$.

explain.text: $f'(0) = -0.3$ and $f'(1) = -0.7$ make 0 and 100% stable; $f'(0.3) = 0.21$ makes 30% a tipping point. A short-rate drift has one stable level instead. A desk finds where a model's drift is zero, and its sign around there, before trusting a simulation.

ideas: A slope field draws the slope $f(t, y)$ at every point; a solution is a curve that follows it.
For $y' = f(y)$ the equilibria are the roots of $f$; the phase line's arrows show which way paths move.
$f'(y^*) < 0$ is stable and $f'(y^*) > 0$ unstable; when $f'(y^*) = 0$, read the signs of $f$ on each side.

formula.name: Stability of an equilibrium
formula.note: Near $y^*$ a small gap nearly obeys $u' = f'(y^*)u$.

summary.trap: Reading stability from the sign of $f$ at the equilibrium (it is 0) or from which one is positive.

quiz.prose: Take $y' = (y - 2)^2$. The only equilibrium is $y = 2$, where $f'(2) = 0$.
quiz.question: How does $y = 2$ behave?

options.text: It attracts from below and repels from above

options.why: Above 2 the slope $(y - 2)^2$ is positive, so paths move up and away.
Below 2 the slope is positive, so paths rise towards 2, not away.
$f'(2) = 0$, so the test is silent; read the signs instead.

feedback.correct: $f \ge 0$ on both sides, so paths rise into 2 from below and away from it above: semi-stable.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the sign of $(y - 2)^2$ just above and just below 2.

explain.text: $(y - 2)^2 > 0$ on both sides, so every nearby path moves up. That is semi-stable, and $f'(2) = 0$ is why the derivative test says nothing. Some nearby paths leave, so in the strict sense it counts as unstable.

byKey.plus: That is $f'(0)$, at the unstable equilibrium.
byKey.zero: That is $f(2)$, the value, not the slope.

explain.text: $f'(2) = -2$, so 2 is stable; $f'(0) = 2$, so 0 is unstable. It is a logistic with $K = 2$.

quiz.prose: Take $y' = y^3 - y$, with equilibria $-1$, 0 and 1.
quiz.question: Which equilibrium is stable?

options.why: Just outside 1, $f > 0$ and paths run upwards, away from 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compute $f'(y) = 3y^2 - 1$ at each equilibrium.

explain.text: $f'(0) = -1$, so 0 attracts; $f'(\pm 1) = 2$, so both outer points repel.

quiz.prose: A slope field looks the same in every column.
quiz.question: Which equation could it belong to?

options.why: The slope changes with $t$ at a fixed height, so the columns differ.
At height 1 the slope is $t$, which changes from column to column.
Here the slope depends only on $t$: the rows look the same, not the columns.

feedback.correct: $\sin y$ has no $t$: an autonomous equation.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Identical columns mean the slope ignores $t$.

explain.text: When the right side depends only on $y$, moving along a row of the field changes nothing. That is an autonomous equation, and its equilibria are horizontal lines.
